subchapters.description: Descriptive text is used to describe a particular person, place, animal, or thing so that readers can form a clear picture of the subject.

material.introduction: Descriptive text is used to describe a particular person, place, animal, or thing so that readers can form a clear picture of the subject. In this unit, students learn how to identify the subject, its characteristics, important details, and the writer’s purpose. A descriptive text normally has an identification section that introduces the subject and a description section that presents characteristics, appearance, achievements, habits, or other relevant details. The description should be organized logically rather than simply listing unrelated facts. When reading a text about an athlete, readers should distinguish objective details from opinions and should infer meaning from context. Descriptive writing also benefits from precise adjectives, noun phrases, simple present tense for general facts, and action verbs where appropriate.
concept: descriptive text identifies and describes a particular subject
identification introduces the subject
description develops characteristics and relevant details
simple present is commonly used for general facts and habitual characteristics
adjectives and precise noun phrases make descriptions clearer
readers should distinguish stated information from inference
effective descriptions select relevant details rather than listing everything
grammar: Simple present: subject + base verb; third-person singular generally takes -s/-es.
Be: am/is/are is used for states and descriptions.
Noun phrase: determiner + adjective(s) + noun, with variations according to context.
Use context to select precise adjectives, verbs, and adverbs.
textStructure: Identification: introduce the subject.
Description: explain relevant characteristics, actions, achievements, or qualities.
example: A strong description might introduce an athlete and then organize physical characteristics, training habits, achievements, and personal qualities into connected paragraphs.

subchapters.description: Describing a person accurately requires more than memorizing adjectives.

material.introduction: Describing a person accurately requires more than memorizing adjectives. Students need to understand how noun phrases, the simple present tense, linking verbs, action verbs, adverbs, and prepositions work together. A noun phrase can combine a determiner, adjective, and noun, such as “a disciplined young athlete.” The simple present is useful for routines, stable characteristics, and generally accepted facts. Linking verbs such as be, seem, and become can connect a subject to a description, while action verbs show what a person does. Context determines which form is appropriate. Students should also learn to avoid vague repetition and choose words that communicate a precise meaning.

subchapters.title: Reading, Inference, and Writing a Description
subchapters.description: Strong reading and writing require students to move beyond locating isolated words.

material.introduction: Strong reading and writing require students to move beyond locating isolated words. When reading a descriptive text, students should identify the main idea, supporting details, references, vocabulary in context, and reasonable inferences. An inference must be supported by information in the text rather than personal assumptions. When writing, students can plan the subject, select relevant characteristics, organize them into identification and description, draft clear sentences, and revise for grammar, coherence, and precision. A good description does not need to contain every fact; it needs the right facts for its purpose and audience.
concept: main idea summarizes the central point of a text
supporting details explain or illustrate the main idea
inference must be supported by textual evidence
reference questions ask what a pronoun or expression refers to
vocabulary in context depends on surrounding information
writing should be organized around a clear purpose
revision checks content, organization, grammar, and word choice
grammar: Simple present: subject + base verb; third-person singular generally takes -s/-es.
Be: am/is/are is used for states and descriptions.
Noun phrase: determiner + adjective(s) + noun, with variations according to context.
Use context to select precise adjectives, verbs, and adverbs.
textStructure: Identification: introduce the subject.
Description: explain relevant characteristics, actions, achievements, or qualities.
example: A strong description might introduce an athlete and then organize physical characteristics, training habits, achievements, and personal qualities into connected paragraphs.
analysis: How can supporting details be identified?
Why is context important for vocabulary?
How should a description be revised?
commonMistakes: Using present continuous for permanent characteristics without a reason.
Listing adjectives without supporting details.
Treating an inference as if it were explicitly stated.
Choosing vocabulary based only on dictionary meaning without context.
strategy: Read the title and first sentences for context.
Mark the main idea and supporting evidence.
Check pronoun references carefully.
For inference questions, eliminate choices that require information outside the text.
In writing, plan identification and description before drafting.
material.summary: A strong descriptive text presents a clear subject, relevant characteristics, precise language, logical organization, and evidence-based interpretation.
learningObjectives: Identify main ideas and supporting evidence in descriptive passages.
Make justified inferences.
Evaluate relevance and objectivity in descriptive writing.
Revise descriptions for coherence and precision.
studyNotes: Main idea is the broad point supported by multiple details.
Evidence should directly support the claim being made.
Inference combines textual evidence with logical reasoning; it is not a guess.
Objective writing benefits from specific, observable information.
checkpoint: Can you cite the detail that supports an inference?
Can you distinguish fact from unsupported praise?
Can you revise a vague description into an evidence-based one?

subchapters.title: Reading and Evaluating Sports Event Reports
subchapters.description: Recount writing depends on accurate past-tense verbs, time connectives, action verbs, and clear references.

material.introduction: Recount writing depends on accurate past-tense verbs, time connectives, action verbs, and clear references. The writer should maintain chronological order and avoid changing tense without a reason. Vocabulary should be selected according to the sport, event, and audience.
concept: A recount has orientation, events, and optional reorientation.
Events are normally arranged chronologically.
A sports report may include score, participants, location, time, and key moments.
A conclusion should be supported by the reported evidence.
grammar: Simple past for completed events.
Time connectives: first, then, after that, finally.
Past verbs should agree with the subject.
Adverbs can clarify time and manner.
textStructure: A recount has orientation, events, and optional reorientation.

A sports report may include score, participants, location, time, and key moments.
A conclusion should be supported by the reported evidence.
example: A well-structured example should show the purpose, relevant language features, and a clear sequence or organization appropriate to the text type.
analysis: Check whether language choices fit audience and context.
commonMistakes: Ignoring context.
Choosing an answer because one word matches the text.
Confusing stated information with inference.
Using grammar forms without considering meaning.
strategy: Read for overall context first.
Locate evidence for every inference.
Eliminate choices that contradict the stimulus.
Review grammar in context rather than as isolated rules.
material.summary: Strong English performance combines text comprehension, language accuracy, vocabulary, organization, and evidence-based reasoning.
learningObjectives: Evaluate event reports using evidence.
Distinguish facts from interpretations.
Identify limitations in a report.
Compare claims with available evidence.
studyNotes: A fact is directly observable or verifiable; an evaluation interprets its significance.
A result alone may have multiple causes.
Good evaluation asks what evidence supports a claim and what remains uncertain.
A balanced report separates observation from judgment.
checkpoint: Can you identify an unsupported evaluation?
Can you suggest evidence that would test a claim?
Can you identify a limitation in a short report?

chapters.description: Materi Bahasa Inggris Kelas 10 Semester 1: Procedure and Health Advice.

subchapters.title: Procedure Text: Healthy Sports Practices
subchapters.description: Evaluating health and sports advice requires evidence-based reasoning.

material.introduction: Evaluating health and sports advice requires evidence-based reasoning. Students should examine whether a claim is supported, whether instructions are complete, and whether the advice fits the stated situation.
concept: Goal states the intended outcome.
Materials or preparation identify what is needed when relevant.
Steps present actions in logical order.
Warnings or notes clarify conditions and safety considerations.
grammar: Imperatives for direct instructions.
Sequence markers such as first, next, then, finally.
Modal verbs such as should and must when appropriate.
Adverbs specify how actions should be performed.
textStructure: Goal states the intended outcome.
Materials or preparation identify what is needed when relevant.
Steps present actions in logical order.
Warnings or notes clarify conditions and safety considerations.
example: A well-structured example should show the purpose, relevant language features, and a clear sequence or organization appropriate to the text type.
analysis: Check whether language choices fit audience and context.
commonMistakes: Ignoring context.
Choosing an answer because one word matches the text.
Confusing stated information with inference.
Using grammar forms without considering meaning.
strategy: Read for overall context first.
Locate evidence for every inference.
Eliminate choices that contradict the stimulus.
Review grammar in context rather than as isolated rules.
material.summary: Strong English performance combines text comprehension, language accuracy, vocabulary, organization, and evidence-based reasoning.
learningObjectives: Identify the goal and sequence of a procedure.
Recognize imperative verbs and sequence markers.
Evaluate precision and safety in instructions.
Revise vague procedural steps.
studyNotes: A procedure is action-oriented and normally has a clear goal.
Imperatives use the base verb to instruct the reader.
Measurements, conditions, and precise verbs improve reproducibility.
Safety-related conditions should be explicit when relevant.

Can you identify vague instructions?
Can you add a useful measurement or condition?
